In nineteen twenty-five, a man sold the Eiffel Tower. Small problem... it wasn't his.
His name was Victor Lustig. A con man with dozens of fake names, and a smile that could sell sand in the desert.
He read that the tower cost Paris a fortune in repairs. So he printed some fake government letterhead,
called himself a deputy director, and invited the city's biggest scrap-metal dealers to a fancy hotel.
The pitch? Top secret. Paris is tearing down the tower, and thousands of tons of iron go to one lucky bidder.
One dealer, André Poisson, bit. Hook, line, and tower. He paid up, cash in hand.
And Lustig? He skipped town with a suitcase full of money.
Poisson was so embarrassed, he never told the police he'd been tricked into buying the Eiffel Tower.
So Lustig came back... and tried to sell it again! This time, a dealer smelled a rat, and Lustig fled to America.
There, he charmed five thousand dollars out of Al Capone, and sold fake money-printing boxes. Then he started printing real fake money.
That last one got him caught. He was sent to Alcatraz. The man who talked his way into selling a tower couldn't talk his way off a rock.
And the tower? Still standing. Still not for sale.
